title: Quarterly Business Review (QBR) Template & Operational Health Checklist for Enterprise Accounts
author: Aisha Patel
content:
Summary:

This document provides a reusable QBR template and an operational health-check runbook tailored for Redwood Inference enterprise customers. The goal is to standardize pre-QBR data collection, meeting agenda, and follow-up actions so Customer Success (CS) and Product/Engineering stakeholders can run consistent, impact-oriented reviews. This is intended for CS Managers, Solutions Engineers, and account owners.

Scope:

- Applies to all enterprise accounts on Dedicated or Private deployments and self-serve hosted accounts that have reached 100k monthly tokens or have an assigned account team.
- Covers technical health metrics, usage economics, feature adoption, incidents and mitigations, and roadmap alignment.
- Does NOT replace security reviews, compliance audits, or billing dispute processes (see related pages).

Before the QBR — Pre-meeting checklist (Owners & timeline):

1. Two weeks prior: CS Manager (owner) creates QBR doc and shares calendar hold.
2. Ten business days prior: Solutions Engineer assembles technical pack (dashboards + raw queries).
3. Five business days prior: Finance/Account Ops confirms invoicing/committed usage data.
4. Two business days prior: Run automated health checks and upload results to the QBR doc.

Automated health checks (what to run and why):

- Latency distribution: p50/p95/p99 for generate and embed APIs (why: detect tail spikes affecting UX).
- Error rates: 4xx vs 5xx split, token-based vs request-based errors (why: surface integration bugs vs runtime failures).
- Token efficiency: avg tokens in vs tokens billed, cache hit ratio (why: cost optimization opportunities).
- Model fallback events: count of automatic fallbacks and fallback latency delta (why: reliability and SLA implications).
- Throughput & saturation: concurrent streams vs GPU pool capacity and queue depth (why: capacity planning).
- Recent incidents: all Sev>=3 incidents in period with MTTD/MTTR metrics.

Required data artifacts (attach to QBR):

- CSV export: token usage by route for the period (columns: date, route, model_version, tokens_in, tokens_out, cost_estimate).
- Dashboard snapshots: daily p95 latency and error-rate chart images.
- Incident timeline: chronological list with brief RCA links.
- Change log: model version pinning and rollout notes in the period.

Example quick queries (source: internal metrics DB) — paste into SE notebook:

-- Top 10 routes by token consumption in period
SELECT route, SUM(tokens_in + tokens_out) as tokens_used
FROM inference_usage
WHERE account_id = 'ACCOUNT_XYZ' AND date >= '2026-01-01'
GROUP BY route
ORDER BY tokens_used DESC
LIMIT 10;

-- p95 latency by model
SELECT model_version, percentile_cont(0.95) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY latency_ms) as p95_latency_ms
FROM request_latencies
WHERE account_id = 'ACCOUNT_XYZ' AND date >= '2026-01-01'
GROUP BY model_version;

Operational health thresholds (SLOs & alert thresholds):

| Metric | SLO target | Alert threshold (page) | Owner |
| --- | ---: | --- | --- |
| API availability (hosted) | 99.95% monthly | < 99.9% sustained 10m | eng-sre |
| p95 generation latency | < 400ms | p95 > 750ms for 30m | eng-serving-runtime |
| Error rate (5xx) | < 0.05% | > 0.25% for 15m | eng-sre |
| Model fallback rate | < 0.1% of requests | > 1% in a day | eng-platform |
| Token billing consistency | 100% accurate | any discrepancy > $500/day | finance-legal |

Health-check runbook (step-by-step):

1. Run the automated dashboard exports and save artifacts to the QBR folder.
2. Verify token billing export against internal cost calc: reconcile top 10 routes.
3. Inspect p95/p99 latency heatmap and flag sequences that show growth (>20% week-over-week).
4. Check prefix/KV cache hit rate — if < 60% for chat routes, add caching config recommendation.
5. Review recent deploys and model changes; correlate deploy timestamps to metric deviations.
6. If error rate spike found, triage: replicable test case -> capture request_id -> escalate to oncall per escalation guide.

QBR meeting agenda (60–90 minutes):

1. Introductions and objectives (5 min) — CS Manager
2. One-slide exec summary (top 3 wins, top 3 risks) (5 min) — CS Manager
3. Usage & economics deep dive (15 min) — Finance/SE: top routes, cost by model, seasonality
4. Reliability & incidents (15 min) — Eng SRE/SE: MTTD/MTTR, recent mitigations, outstanding risks
5. Feature adoption & product feedback (10 min) — Product/CS: experiments, quality regressions
6. Roadmap alignment and ask list (10 min) — Customer success & Product: timelines & impact
7. Action items, owners, and timing (5–10 min) — CS Manager closes

Post-QBR deliverables and follow-up (owners & SLAs):

- Action tracker created within 48 hours (owner: CS Manager).
- Engineering commit for high-priority reliability fixes defined within 7 days or logged in product backlog with priority tag.
- Monthly checkpoints for long-running items, status updates posted to QBR doc.

Template for QBR exec summary (one paragraph):

[Customer] continues to grow usage across routes X and Y (+22% MoM) with 84% of tokens consumed by model m-v1. Performance remained within SLOs for the period (p95=320ms), but two incidents in January increased MTTD and require a deployment policy change to improve fallback behavior. Action items: (1) enable prefix caching on chat routes (owner: SE, due in 14 days), (2) prioritize model rollback testing (owner: eng-platform).

Common integration checklists (for SEs during QBR prep):

- Verify SDK versions in customer code (JS/Python) and recommend upgrades for known bugfixes.
- Confirm retry/backoff strategies and idempotency for client requests.
- Confirm that customers use model pinning where deterministic output is required.

Known caveats & workarounds (short list for QBR discussion):

- Large batch inference on Dedicated pools can exhibit higher p99 latency under autoscaling transitions. Workaround: pre-warm additional nodes for predictable high-throughput windows.
- Quantized model outputs may exhibit minor tokenization differences vs FP32; advise regression tests on golden prompt sets before rolling to prod.
- Third-party CDN misconfigurations can cause 4xx errors that mimic client SDK bugs — validate request_id and raw request headers before escalating.

Risk levels and escalation path (summary):

- Risk tier 1 (Critical business impact): finance-impacting billing errors, data leakage, or sustained outages -> escalate to Eng SRE Lead and CS Director within 30 minutes.
- Risk tier 2 (High): frequent fallbacks or model quality regressions that materially affect UX -> notify Eng Platform and Product; schedule hotfix/rollback within 48 hours.
- Risk tier 3 (Medium): feature adoption gaps and non-urgent performance tuning -> track in backlog and review quarterly.

Appendix: sample slide list and artifacts to attach

- Slide 1: Executive summary + 3 bullets (wins/risks)
- Slide 2: Top routes & cost-by-model chart
- Slide 3: Latency curves (p50/p95/p99) and anomaly annotations
- Slide 4: Incident timeline + RCA links
- Slide 5: Roadmap & open asks with owners
- Attachments: CSV exports, dashboard images, relevant incident postmortems

How to reuse this template:

1. Copy this file into the customer's QBR folder and replace placeholders (ACCOUNT_XYZ, dates).
2. Attach generated artifacts from dashboards and the metrics SQL exports.
3. Tag the QBR doc with the customer-wide label and assign reviewers two weeks before the meeting.
